market_scan.market_size_text: The addressable pool is much wider than microwave OEMs: all industrial thermal-equipment manufacturers who could add microwave/RF modules to dryers, kilns, ovens and process lines. Adjacent markets are large — industrial dryers ~$5-8B/yr, industrial drying ovens ~$3B/yr — versus only ~$1.4-1.6B/yr currently captured by dedicated microwave equipment, which quantifies the headroom for microwave integration. The simulation/software slice an 'access' product could initially capture is small (~$20-100M/yr) but the mechanism is catalytic: lowering the barrier to entry expands the microwave market itself. Macro tailwind: process-heat electrification/decarbonization programs (US DOE Industrial Heat Shot, EU projects) explicitly name microwave systems.

regions.Europe: ~$1.5-3B adjacent thermal-equipment market (dryers+ovens subset); strong OEM density in DE/IT/FR
regions.Asia: ~$3-4B adjacent market (~40%+ of dryer demand; largest OEM pool, mostly mid-tier)

market_scan.target_customers_text: Thousands of industrial equipment OEMs and system integrators (drying, thermal processing, food/pharma/chemical machinery) have no in-house RF/microwave competence. The motivated subset — those facing electrification pressure or customer pull for faster/volumetric heating — is realistically ~300-1,000 companies globally. They are reachable via general process-equipment channels and OEM-component suppliers, but each sale requires substantial education: the CalNEXT market study identifies 'knowledge and awareness' alongside cost and process-integration as the primary adoption barriers. A tool alone will not convert this segment; tool + application engineering service will.
market_scan.players_text: No one sells 'microwave integration made accessible' as a product. What exists: (a) generalist EM/CFD suites at expert price/skill level (Ansys, CST, COMSOL), (b) cloud CAE platforms (SimScale, Ansys cloud) that remove the compute barrier but not the expertise barrier, (c) microwave component/generator vendors (Muegge, Sairem, Richardson, e2v) who effectively act as the integration path today via application labs and OEM supply, and (d) a fragmented layer of MW consultants and university labs. So the competitive field is indirect: ProSeed would compete with 'hire/borrow expertise' rather than with another software vendor.

technologies.name: Expert-level generalist EM/multiphysics tools (Ansys HFSS, CST, COMSOL RF)
technologies.how: The theoretically-correct path: model applicator + product + thermal coupling; in practice requires hiring or contracting EM specialists plus $10-70k seats.
technologies.performance: Validated accuracy; complete design freedom; combined license+expert cost easily ~$150-300k first year for a new OEM
technologies.limits: This is the barrier, not the solution: steep learning curve, no microwave-heating defaults, and no guidance on dielectric data or ISM compliance — unusable for a first-time OEM without external help

technologies.name: Template/app-based simulation (COMSOL Application Builder + compiled apps, QuickWave BHM projects)
technologies.how: Experts encapsulate validated models behind simplified UIs (product dimensions, moisture, throughput → field/uniformity results); COMSOL Server/Compiler can distribute apps to non-specialists.
technologies.performance: Proven pattern (ITW built internal MW-heating apps on COMSOL; frozen-sandwich simulator case study); reduces user skill need while keeping full-wave accuracy
technologies.limits: Requires an expert to build each app (service-heavy); per-domain templates for industrial applicators do not exist off-the-shelf; licensing costs for app distribution add up

technologies.name: Cloud/browser simulation platforms (SimScale, Ansys Gateway/AWS, COMSOL Server)
technologies.how: Browser access to solvers on elastic HPC; removes workstation and license-infrastructure barriers.
technologies.performance: On-demand compute at ~$ per run vs ~$50k seats; market analysts cite cloud delivery as a key growth driver
technologies.limits: Solves the compute-access problem only; user still needs EM model-building expertise and material data — the actual bottleneck for non-expert OEMs

technologies.name: Component/vendor-led integration (Muegge, SAIREM, Richardson, e2v, CPI generators + applicators + application labs)
technologies.how: OEM buys standard generators, waveguides and applicators and relies on the component vendor's engineering support and test labs for integration.
technologies.performance: The dominant real-world path today; vendors advertise application support across sectors; SAIREM alone cites ~5,000 machines installed
technologies.limits: Locks the OEM into one supplier's catalogue and margins; limited physics insight into the OEM's specific product/load; vendors have no incentive to optimize outside their component envelope

technologies.name: Consultants, university labs and feasibility testing (AMPERE/IMPI networks)
technologies.how: Contract research: dielectric measurement, pilot trials on vendor/university equipment, bespoke applicator design.
technologies.performance: Real expertise on demand; typical feasibility projects ~$20-100k and months of calendar time
technologies.limits: Not scalable, knowledge does not accumulate in the OEM; each new application restarts the same learning curve

technologies.name: Open-source EM codes (openEMS, MEEP, gprMax)
technologies.how: Free FDTD/FEM solvers, script-driven, usable as the engine inside a guided product.
technologies.performance: Zero license cost; adequate physics for 2.45 GHz cavities; growing validation literature
technologies.limits: Expert-only interfaces, no heating/materials workflow, no support — not viable for target customers directly, but a viable compute backend for a ProSeed product

tech_baseline.why_better_text: The barrier for non-microwave OEMs is not solver access — it is the missing expertise and the missing dielectric/compliance data. ProSeed can beat incumbents by packaging what the component vendors and consultants sell implicitly (validated applicator templates, measured dielectric database, ISM/IEC-60519-6-aware design rules) into a guided tool-plus-service product: feasibility answer in days instead of a $50k study, then a designed applicator the OEM integrates with any generator supplier. Because ProSeed owns real microwave equipment and process data, its templates start calibrated rather than generic — a structural advantage over both cloud CAE platforms and generalist EM suites for this novice segment.
